column1: What three primitive operations does every DSP effect (EQ, reverb, compression, distortion) reduce to?
column2: Delay (store a past sample), scale (multiply by a coefficient), and sum (add signals together).

column1: At a 44.1 kHz sample rate, what is the Nyquist frequency, and what happens to content above it?
column2: 22.05 kHz (half the sample rate). Content above it aliases — folds back into the audible range as inharmonic noise unrelated to the source.

column1: Why do professional distortion/saturation plugins oversample (4x–16x) internally?
column2: Nonlinear processing (clipping) generates harmonics far above Nyquist; oversampling pushes those harmonics higher before filtering and decimating back down, so they get filtered out before they can fold back (alias) into the audible range.

column1: How much dynamic range does each bit of bit depth roughly add, and what are the typical values for 16-bit vs 24-bit?
column2: ~6.02 dB per bit. 16-bit ≈ 96 dB dynamic range; 24-bit ≈ 144 dB.

column1: Why do modern DAWs process audio internally at 32-bit or 64-bit float instead of 16-bit integer?
column2: Integer arithmetic truncates (not rounds), causing quantization error to accumulate over many gain/EQ operations; floating point essentially eliminates this concern until final export.

column1: What is dither, and what is the rule for when to apply it?
column2: Dither is a tiny amount of noise added before truncating bit depth (e.g., 24-bit→16-bit) to decorrelate quantization error from the signal, turning audible grainy artifacts into an inaudible flat noise floor. Rule: dither once, only at the final bit-depth-reduction step, never earlier in the chain.

column1: In the DFT, what is the formula for frequency bin spacing (Δf), and what does increasing N do to it?
column2: Δf = fs / N. Increasing N (FFT size) gives finer (smaller) frequency resolution, but smears the analysis over a longer time window.

column1: What is the time-frequency uncertainty trade-off in FFT analysis, and how do you choose FFT size accordingly?
column2: You cannot get perfect time and frequency localization simultaneously. Use a short FFT (512–1024 samples) for precise transient timing (e.g., drum attacks); use a long FFT (8192–16384 samples) for precise frequency resolution (e.g., bass pitch).

column1: In the general difference equation y[n] = b0·x[n] + ... - a1·y[n-1] - ..., what distinguishes an FIR filter from an IIR filter?
column2: If all feedback coefficients (a_k) are zero, it's FIR (feedforward only, no poles). If any a_k is nonzero, it's IIR (has feedback/poles).

column1: What is the stability condition for an IIR filter's poles, and why is a pole at |p| = 0.9999 risky despite being technically stable?
column2: Every pole must satisfy |p| < 1 to be stable. A pole at 0.9999 is stable on paper but rings for seconds and can become unstable after coefficient rounding in fixed-precision implementations.

column1: What three invariants must every digital filter design satisfy, per the curriculum's core checklist?
column2: 1) Causality — output depends only on current/past input (true real-time constraint). 2) Stability — all poles satisfy |p| < 1. 3) Sampling — content above fs/2 aliases and cannot be repaired after the fact; design stopbands below Nyquist.

column1: Why must every feedback coefficient in a delay line (e.g., for echo/reverb) stay strictly below 1.0 in magnitude?
column2: The feedback coefficient acts as a pole: inside the unit circle (|g| < 1) it decays (stable, lush echo); at or above 1.0 it oscillates or grows unbounded, causing the effect to scream and clip.
